page.ogDescription: 175°C equals 347°F. Fan oven, air fryer and Gas Mark equivalents, plus UK baking times and USDA safe temperatures.
page.tagline: Convert 175°C to Fahrenheit, find fan oven and air fryer equivalents, British baking times at 175°C, and USDA safe internal temperatures.
page.customIntro: 175 degrees Celsius equals 347 degrees Fahrenheit, calculated as (175 × 9/5) + 32 = 347°F. It is a moderate oven temperature loved for gentle, even baking: Victoria sponge, Bakewell tart and slow-roast chicken all turn out beautifully at 175°C. For fan ovens or air fryers, reduce to 155°C (311°F). Note that 175°C is not the same as the American 350°F — see the comparison below.

about.title: About 175°C / 347°F: Why Bakers Choose a Gentler Heat
about.paragraph1: 175°C (347°F) sits 20°C below the standard 180°C baking temperature, and that margin changes how bakes behave. It is still well above the 140°C (285°F) threshold where the Maillard reaction begins, so crusts colour and flavours develop — but the gentler heat gives thick sponges and dense batters time to set their structure before the outside finishes. That is why many bakers drop a Victoria sponge or Bakewell tart to 175°C: the top rises evenly instead of doming and cracking, and the centre cooks through without the edges drying out.
about.paragraph2: Home ovens are often inaccurate: real-world testing shows many run 25–50°F (14–28°C) hotter or cooler than the dial says. An oven set to 175°C might actually be running at 150°C or 200°C, which matters far more at this temperature than the 3°F gap between 175°C and 350°F. A $10–20 oven thermometer is the single most effective tool for consistent results — place it on the middle rack while preheating and cook to the measured temperature, not the dial.

cards.title: British Bakes at 175°C
items: Victoria sponge: a gentle 175°C gives an even rise and flat top, ideal for stacking and filling.
Bakewell tart and millionaire's shortbread: the lower heat sets the filling and caramel without over-browning the base.
Gingerbread, flapjacks and traybakes: slow, even caramelisation of sugar and syrup without burnt edges.

cards.title: Slow Roasting and Savoury Cooking
items: Slow-roast chicken: 175°C for 20 minutes per 450g plus 20 minutes keeps the breast juicy while the legs turn tender.
Root vegetables and roast potatoes: 45–60 minutes renders the fat slowly for a crispy outside and fluffy inside.
Casseroles, braises and baked pasta: thorough, even heating for dishes that cook for an hour or more.

cards.title: Delicate and Precision Tasks
items: Toasting nuts and seeds: 10–15 minutes at 175°C develops flavour without scorching — check every 5 minutes.
Drying herbs and fleur de sel: a low fan setting at 150–175°C removes moisture while preserving colour.
Reheating roast dinners and pies: restores crispness at 175°C without drying the filling.

bakingTimes.title: Baking Times at 175°C (347°F)
bakingTimes.intro: Typical times for popular British bakes at 175°C in a conventional oven. Always check doneness with a skewer or thermometer rather than relying on time alone, and rotate the tin once halfway through for even colour.

rows.doneness: Skewer clean, top springs back, edges just leaving the tin
Pastry golden, filling set with a slight wobble
Base firm, caramel bubbly, chocolate glossy and set
Springy to the touch, cracked surface, skewer with few crumbs
Golden edges, centre still slightly soft — firms on cooling
Internal temp 74°C / 165°F (USDA) in the thickest part
Deep golden, crisp outside, fluffy inside
Even golden colour, nutty smell — check every 5 minutes

bakingTimes.note: Times assume a conventional oven. For fan ovens or air fryers, reduce the time by 10–15% and check doneness early.

foodSafety.title: USDA Safe Internal Temperatures
foodSafety.intro: Oven temperature is not the same as food internal temperature. A slow roast at 175°C is gentle on meat, which makes a thermometer essential — the USDA recommends these minimum internal temperatures, measured in the thickest part of the food.
foodSafety.source: Source: USDA FoodSafety.gov (last reviewed November 2024). Rest meat for 3 minutes after cooking; always verify with a food thermometer.

whatNotToBake.title: What NOT to Bake at 175°C
whatNotToBake.intro: 175°C is a gentle all-rounder, but several foods need either higher heat for structure or lower heat for delicate textures. Using 175°C for these leads to soggy bases, pale crusts or cracked custards.

items.reason: Use 100–150°C — 175°C browns and cracks the delicate structure before it dries out.
Use 190–200°C — needs high heat for steam to separate the layers.
Use 200–220°C — needs high heat for oven spring and a blistered crust.
Use 220°C or above — a 175°C base stays pale and doughy.
Use 150–160°C in a water bath — 175°C scrambles the eggs and curdles the custard.
Use 220°C — scones need a hot oven for the fast rise that creates their signature layers.

troubleshooting.title: Baking Troubleshooting at 175°C
troubleshooting.intro: If your bakes at 175°C are not turning out right, the problem is usually oven accuracy, rack position or tin choice. These are the most common issues at this temperature and how to fix them.

rows.cause: Oven runs hotter than the dial, or batter overfilled
rows.fix: Verify with an oven thermometer; if the oven is accurate, drop to 165°C and fill tins no more than two-thirds full.

rows.cause: Oven runs hot, or tin too close to the element
rows.fix: Move the rack to the centre, lower to 165°C, and extend the time rather than raising the heat.

rows.cause: Oven runs cool, or the door was opened too early
rows.fix: Raise to 180°C and keep the door shut for the first 20 minutes — 175°C is unforgiving of cool ovens.

rows.cause: Filling too wet, or base under-baked before filling was added
rows.fix: Blind bake the base for 10–12 minutes first, and use a thick jam layer rather than a thin, runny one.

rows.cause: Cooked too long at too high a temperature for the size of the bird
rows.fix: Cover the breast with foil for the first hour and pull the bird at 74°C internal — it will rise 2–3°C while resting.

rows.problem: Roast potatoes are pale and soft
rows.cause: Fat not hot enough, or the oven is crowded
rows.fix: Use one tray per batch, render at 175°C for 45 minutes, then blast at 220°C for 10 minutes to crisp.

rows.cause: Underbaked in the middle, or too much syrup for the dry ingredients
rows.fix: Give it another 8–10 minutes and test the centre with a skewer — a few moist crumbs mean done; wet batter means more time.

faq.question: What is 175 degrees Celsius in Fahrenheit?
faq.answer: 175 degrees Celsius equals 347 degrees Fahrenheit. The conversion formula is °F = (°C × 9/5) + 32, so multiply 175 by 1.8 to get 315, then add 32 for 347°F. This is a moderate oven temperature that suits gentle baking, slow roasting and anything that needs even, thorough heat.

faq.question: Is 175°C the same as 350°F?
faq.answer: No. 175°C equals 347°F, while 350°F converts to 176.7°C — a difference of about 3°F (2°C). For most bakes the gap does not matter, but for delicate sponges it is worth using the exact Celsius figure rather than rounding up to 350°F, because the slightly hotter oven can dome and crack a thick batter.

faq.question: What is 175°C in a fan oven or air fryer?
faq.answer: Reduce by 20°C to 155°C (311°F). Fan circulation cooks roughly 20% faster, so also cut the cooking time by 10–15%. In an air fryer, preheat fully, cook in a single layer, and shake the basket halfway through so food browns evenly without the edges drying out.

faq.question: What Gas Mark is 175°C?
faq.answer: 175°C falls between Gas Mark 3 (170°C) and Gas Mark 4 (180°C). In practice, recipes round 175°C up to Gas Mark 4, which officially equals 180°C (350°F) — close enough for cakes, tarts and roasts. On older gas ovens without precise markings, Gas Mark 4 checked with an oven thermometer is the safest setting.

faq.question: What can I bake at 175°C?
faq.answer: 175°C is ideal for Victoria sponge, Bakewell tart, millionaire's shortbread, gingerbread and flapjacks, plus slow-roast chicken and root vegetables. It suits any bake that benefits from gentle, even heat rather than a fast rise — thick batters set through without doming, and slow roasts stay juicy while their edges caramelise.
